newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico stocks close up in late recovery.
newsitem.headline: Mexico stocks close up in late recovery.

text.p: Mexican stocks rebounded from a mid-session bout of profit-taking to close slightly up on Monday on gains by market stragglers in a session dulled by a lack of foreign investors, traders and analysts said.
"Investors are going for illiquid stocks, we could say they're giving the market some turnover," an equity analyst said.
The leading IPC share index closed up 6.43 points, or 0.17 percent, at 3,739.59. Volume totaled 102.3 million shares traded, but traders noted about one-third were in unrepresentative cross trades.
Traders said volume was below many recent sessions as U.S. markets were partly closed for Martin Luther King Jr. Day.

"The market was very dull. You could tell there were few foreign investors...I think we'll see more intraday profit-taking for the market to gather strength," said a trader from the Bursamex brokerage.

The IPC dipped to a midsession low of 3,708.76 on what traders said was profit-taking. Nonetheless, traders said a late recovery in the Dow Jones, which ended up 0.16 percent to 6,843.87 points, was not the driving force behind a similar move in Mexico.
"The Dow Jones helped us because it enhanced confidence, but it was not the main reason," a trader said.
On the broad market, 113 stocks changed hands, with gainers outnumbering sliders 55 to 32.

Traders said the gainers' list was headed by relatively illiquid stocks that had lagged behind the recent market rally, like autoparts maker Isasa and publishers Gfesa, which ended up three and 19 centavos, respectively, at 32 centavos and 2.03 pesos.
Another leading gainer was technology firm Acerla, up 1.90 pesos to 29.40 pesos.
Dealers said Acerla was bolstered by the announcement it had signed a letter of agreement to buy a Brazilian computer manufacturer and distributor.
Financial group Banacci and mining firm Autlan headed the sliders after declining 62 and 30 centavos, respectively, at 15.80 and 8.60 pesos on profit-taking, dealers said.
